abstract:
Species diversity has become of more importance to ecological community surveys and 
conservation efforts globally. Use of such methods of assessing species in target groups of 
particular concern, such as herpetofauna, have increased in frequency in recent decades, 
incorporating mathematical indices and measures in an attempt to analyze community 
composition as a trend over time. The goal of this study was to report herpetofauna species found 
in the region, their diversity, dominance and rarity, richness, and other measures throughout the 
four separate survey trips, showing trends over the periods of time in order to better inform the 
timing and methods of the survey in future years. Ex-situ data analysis of the detections over 
four years thus far have found 86 herpetofauna individuals across 26 distinct species. Reptilian 
species make up the larger portion of detections than amphibian, with a ratio of detections and 
relative abundance of 1.39:1, respectively. Dominant species across trip years included the 
southern two-lined salamander, the southern cricket frog, and the little brown skink. Dominant 
species across seasons included the Mississippi slimy salamander, southern cricket frog, and 
little brown skink. Highest herpetofauna abundance was found in 2018 and in the fall season, 
while highest species richness was detected in 2018 and in the spring season. Species evenness 
was maximized in 2019 and in the fall season. Shannon-Weiner and Simpson’s Diversity were 
both maximized in the 2018 and spring trips and lowest in the 202

and fall trips overall. 
Diversity of amphibians in particular was maximized in 2022 and in fall, while diversity of 
reptiles in particular was maximized in 2018 and in spring season. Reptiles were detected at 
higher average substrate temperatures and similar air temperatures to amphibians. The highest 
and lowest temperatures at detection for amphibians were lower than those for reptiles when 
adjusting for the summer season anomaly found. Deviations from expectations formed from 
knowledge on herpetological distribution, ecology, and life history were found in herpetofauna 
abundance and diversity in particular seasons, while other measures of richness, abundance, and 
evenness met predictions. This survey thus far gave insight into the state of the herpetofauna 
community in the study region, creating a baseline for comparison in continuation of the study. 
The value of this extended study thus far will prove critical in moving forward in herpetofauna 
conservation, particularly with attention to bias and improvements to methods found in the past 
four years.  
 
Introduction 
 
Biodiversity has become one of the most frequently used evaluation measures for 
ecological communities, habitats, and their species (Dodd 1992, Iknayan et al. 2014, Martensson 
2016). Biodiversity has been defined to include “diversity within species, between species, and 
of ecosystems” (Martensson 2016). Diversity of species within a particular habitat or compared 
between habitats or ecosystems has only increased in use within the biological research areas, 
 
Muia 3
arising as a prominent topic in the fields of life-history evolution and community ecology, and 
has even become a measure indicating population, ecosystem, or environmental health (Dodd 
1992, Martensson 2016, Winter et al. 2013). Diversity of species has arisen as a significant 
aspect of the fundamental definition of community, ecosystem, and ecology, and has been more 
realized as an important facet in environmental science as a greater study for a multitude of 
reasons (Maretnsson 2016). Estimates of species diversity as a parameter, and, hand-in hand, 
other measures of species richness, abundance, evenness, as trends over time, have become 
altogether central to community and larger ecosystem ecology, elucidating dynamics that govern 
ecological communities, linking ecosystem services and keystone, indicator, and signal species, 
ecosystem function, ecological monitoring, comparative community studies, and spatial 
community patterns, among others (Iknayan et al. 2014, Laurencio and Fitzgerald 2010, Moritz 
et al. 2005, Winter et al. 2013). While numerous classes are the focus of diversity-related 
surveys, herpetofauna are one group highly targeted by such studies and have a growing body of 
literature surrounding them as of late.  
 
Herpetofauna, or amphibians and reptiles, the focus of the field of herpetology, have been 
a vertebrate group of particular concern and interest to ecologists and conservation biologists in 
recent decades (Gibbons and Stangel 1999, Leyte-Manrique at al. 2019, Olson and Saenz 2013, 
Urbina-Cardona 2008, USGS 2022). These two groups are critical to the maintenance of 
biological diversity, fulfill numerous functional roles, and are heralds of the environmental 
quality of the habitats in which they live (Gibbons and Stangel 1999). As of late, these species 
have garnered concerns surrounding their declining ecological state, along with their habitats. 
Species of both herpetological classes occupy similar habitats and are equally vulnerable to 
habitat degradation, their currently known global, anthropogenic threats, to observed and 
 
Muia 4
expected population declines, and to the possibility of extinction (Ruthven et al. 2002, USGS 
2022, Whitfield Gibbons et al. 2000). The world’s reptiles and amphibians face stressors unique 
to them with known – climate change, habitat degradation and fragmentation, agricultural 
intensification, urbanization, pollution, and disease – origins that will only continue to bring 
about declines, extirpations, and extinctions if not rectified (Ghosh and Basu 2020, Rabbe et al. 
2022, USGS 2022, Whitfield Gibbons et al. 2000). Herpetofauna, therefore, have been the focus 
of much species and community surveying along with conservation efforts attempting to 
alleviate the stress and declines to these vulnerable populations worldwide. It has become 
necessary and significantly more common in recent decades for the composition, distribution, 
and especially the diversity of reptiles and amphibians to be studied to assess deviations from 
expected patterns, evaluate ecological state, estimate causes of decline, and to inform species and 
habitat conservation priorities and tactics (Leyte-Manrique et al. 2019, Russell et al. 2002, 
Urbina-Cardona 2008).  
 
Detection studies and diversity assessment have increasingly become a critical 
component of studies assessing herpetofauna in particular – their status, abundance and 
distribution, habitats, and priorities in conservation. Such studies largely employ methods such 
as Simpson’s Diversity Index and the newer-developed Shannon-Weiner index to describe an 
ecosystem’s diversity with a value instead of measuring solely relative abundance of species. 
Studies also utilize other species measures as trends over time such as abundance, dominance, 
rarity, evenness, and richness in order to inform ecologists on the composition, state, health, and 
conservation threat of specific herpetological communities (Briones Jr. 2017, Kumar et al. 2022, 
Smith and Berry 2010, Wilson and Gownaris 2022). Considering that herpetofauna species are 
notoriously difficult and inconsistent to detect, challenging to monitor, knowledge and surveys in 
 
Muia 5
many of their critical regions remain incomplete, their habitats have been largely degraded or 
fragmented to varying extents, species have differed levels of threat or decline, little information 
is available on how factors affect their species assemblages, and raw counts or similar metrics 
are highly susceptible to bias, these two groups of species are and have been a major suitable 
target for the newer-developed detection, management, and conservation strategies utilizing 
species diversity indices and other related species trend measures (Behangana et al. 2020, Kumar 
et al. 2022, Kusamba 2019, Smith and Berry 2010).  
As mentioned, herpetofauna across the board experience heightened levels of threat and 
vulnerability to a wide variety of factors causing their global declines, namely habitat 
disturbance and fragmentation due to anthropogenic, climate, or other origins (Ruthven et al. 
2002, USGS 2022, Whitfield Gibbons et al. 2000). Diversity index studies taking into account 
abundances, evenness, distribution, dominance, and other factors allow spatial status and 
occurrence assessment, comparative studies among and between numerous fragmented habitats, 
species response to environmental disturbances or degradations, contributions of specific habitats 
to overall populations and species continuation, species assemblages in differing landscapes, 
species dominance or rarity, and identification of species, habitats, and populations most at risk, 
therefore contributing to overall knowledge and prioritization of those when it comes to 
allocating conservation attention, funding, and efforts (Ghosh, Kusamba 2019, Laurencio and 
Fitz, Leyte-Manrique et al. Mortiz). A major 2019 study on herpetofauna in the Democratic 
Republic of the Congo utilized long term herpetological surveys including species occurrence 
and relevant diversity indices, including Shannon-Weiner index, along with richness, rarity, 
presence of threatened species, and endemism in order to direct conservation awareness and 
governmental and organizational efforts to appropriate habitats. This ultimately led to the 
 
Muia 6
identification and creation of ten sites as the proposed new Protected Areas for reaching the 
government’s national conservation targets necessary for conserving the rich biodiversity of the 
country (Kusamba 2019). Another major study in 2019 and one in 2002 concluded the 
significant importance of herpetological diversity (both using Shannon-Weiner diversity index), 
abundance, and taxonomic distinctness of environments with different levels of disturbance in 
the identification and development of efficient conservation routes and strategies for reptiles and 
amphibians in Salvatierra, Guanajuato, Mexico and coastal South Carolina, respectively (Leyte-
Manrique et al. 2019, Russell et al. 2002). It is clear that species diversity and its associated 
measures are principal to informing herpetological conservation on the basis of their largest 
threats – habitat degradation, fragmentation, lack of knowledge and historical surveys, and 
anthropogenic disturbance, among many others.  
The in-situ field portion of this study, occurring over a period of four years in Northern 
Mississippi, is a herpetological survey which then had mathematical indices and measures 
incorporated in an attempt to analyze community composition, species diversity, and other 
species measures as trends over time. The goal of this study was to ultimately report 
herpetofauna species found in the region, their presence and detection, variation, diversity, 
abundance, dominance and rarity, richness, and other measures throughout the four separate 
survey trips, showing trends over the periods of time in order to better inform the timing and 
methods for continuation and amplification of the survey in future years. It also emphasizes 
deviations from expectations for these parameters, giving insight into the state of the 
herpetofauna community in the study region, creating a baseline for comparison in continuation 
of the study, and noting areas of conservational concern.

Methods 
 
The goal of each trip within the overall study was a survey of the herpetological species 
in the area using varying in-situ detection methods and later ex-situ data analytical methods. 
In-situ Fieldwork Methods 
 
In-situ methods occurred in remote upland Northern Mississippi over the course of four 
years: 2018, 2019, 2021, and 2022. The 2018 trips and data collection occurred in mid-April, 
again in late May and early June, and a third time in later June. The 2019 trip and data collection 
occurred in late March and early April. The 2021 and 2022 trips and data collection both 
occurred in early October. The habitat of the study region is mixed prairie and field of retired 
farmland, hardwood forest with both flat and sloped landscape, and scattered standing water and 
streams with riparian habitat.  
Herpetological surveying was carried out utilizing multiple various methods of detection 
targeting different types of reptiles and amphibians. Coverboards, ranging from 3x5 feet to 
approximately 6x10 feet and made of either corrugated tin or plywood, were arranged within the 
study area at varying elevations, slopes, landscapes, and amount of canopy cover (boards utilized 
ranged from no to full cover). These boards were placed mainly away from larger sources of 
water, being positioned within either leaf litter and soil forest floor or grassy field. This type of 
detection method targets both reptiles and amphibians due to their shared characteristic of having 
strong, distinct hygrothermal microclimate p
references:
(Grant et al. 2001). The habitat of 
herpetofauna across the board is wholly based upon the heat and moisture, or hygrothermal, 
nature of the substrate and air around them, with each species occupying a very specific 
microclimate exhibiting those particular levels to them (Grant et al. 2001). Coverboards offer the 
manmade creation of a variety of microclimates placed where they may not have existed 
naturally, therefore valuable to designing a successful study region for a survey of this type. 
 
Muia 8
However, coverboards in such surveys target reptiles more in particular, due to the heat 
absorbing nature of the boards’ large surface area, attracting these more highly ectothermic, less 
permeable-skinned, and drier climate species more resistant to desiccation. Reptiles are more 
likely to move under these boards and obtain heat directly from the board above them, 
particularly when the ground below is drier, than amphibians are expected to (Grant et al. 2001). 
However, this method does not entirely exclude amphibian species, as some of the larger, thicker 
wood coverboards harbored a decent amount of moisture under them, particularly if the board 
was atop soil and especially if it was under a larger amount of canopy cover causing more 
shading and slightly cooler temperatures. This aspect allows for species more permeable-skinned 
and more vulnerable to desiccation to move to them for a heat source without too dry of a 
substrate. Coverboards were checked daily in each trip of the study by approaching and carefully 
lifting each board away from the individual or group of individuals present as a safety 
precaution, and then quickly assessing the area under the board and trapping any animals found. 
Carpets were used similarly, but only two of these were placed in the study region. These fabric-
like mats were approximately 12x12 feet each, both positioned on a hillier landscape directly 
atop soil substrate and under approximately 30% canopy cover. These carpets target both types 
of herpetofauna, rapidly absorbing more heat due to their material and higher sun exposure, as 
well as harboring larger amounts of moisture between mat and substrate after a precipitation 
event. The by-hand trapping of the study made up the largest portion of detection methods used, 
detecting and trapping herpetofauna by physically displacing parts of or objects in the landscape 
acting as natural “coverboards” in an attempt to reveal animals below. These included natural 
parts of the animals’ habitats, mainly “dead and down” tree branches and trunks both newly 
downed or decomposing, leaf litter, rocks, and scrap wood, metal, and other materials not 
 
Muia 9
necessarily placed to carry out the function of a coverboard (present mainly near the garages 
throughout the study area). This detection method was carried out throughout the day on each 
day of each trip, starting early in the morning and continuing until evening as the region was 
traveled and other forms of traps were checked. This method targeted both kinds of 
herpetofauna, as both utilize such objects and parts of their natural landscape and habitat to 
obtain or conduct heat and moisture. A reptile may be present under a rock in direct sunlight in 
order to conduct heat, while an amphibian may be present when a moist, decomposing log is 
overturned. This detection and trapping method was carried out in all types of habitat across the 
study region, not being limited to drier or wetter conditions or a particular type of substrate, 
canopy cover, etc. Visual detections also included a significant portion of detections which also 
led to hand-trapping. This type of detection method, unlike the last, involved hand trapping 
herpetofauna after purely visual detection only, without the physical disturbance of any piece of 
the environment involved. This method is one which does favor reptilian over amphibian 
species. Reptilian species, being less resistant to desiccation and therefore less reliant on 
moisture, shade, or cooler temperatures, use the behavior of basking frequently in order to 
maximize the amount of heat conducted or obtained from their environment. Basking is the main 
behavior leading to visual encounters and detection without disturbing or physically altering the 
environment, as individuals must be exposed in order to carry out this heat exchange with their 
habitat. It is not common for amphibious species to bask, but is a behavior shared by almost 
every type of reptile. Finally, ProMar 250 hoop funnel nets were employed in two major bodies 
of water within the study region, both standing, freshwater ponds. Two traps were placed and 
secured within the smaller pond while the number of traps in the larger body of water ranged 
from 3 to 6 traps. These were baited with canned cat food, replaced each day as the traps were 
 
Muia 10
pulled in and checked daily for each day of each trip. This detection method clearly targets both 
aquatic reptilian and amphibian species rather than the strictly terrestrial targets of the other 
detection methods.  
 
As each detection method was checked or carried out, any herpetofauna found or caught 
were placed into appropriate containers, either plastic jars or fabric snake bags based on species 
and size. Turtles were placed in snake bags, while smaller reptiles and amphibians were mainly 
contained within the jars. While still in-situ, data based on the environment was collected and 
recorded, along with a number identifying the animal with its data sheet. For each capture, while 
still in-situ, field identification was carried out based on initial impressions and prior 
herpetological knowledge, and then date, time of capture, latitude and longitude of capture site, 
substrate and habitat type, and measures of air, substrate, and ground (if different) temperatures 
in degrees Celsius, percent relative humidity, windspeed, and canopy cover percentage were 
recorded with varying equipment, along with notes of any distinguishing characteristics of the 
individual or any comments on the capture. Each capture site was also marked in the GPS units 
as a specific numbered waypoint corresponding with the animal and data sheet. Animals in 
appropriate containers were secured by members of the group and were taken from the field to, 
in the case of this study, the cabin in the study region, for processing and further ex-situ data 
collection. 
 
Once present at the processing site, animals were matched with their data sheets from the 
field by number, and then handled and assessed further one by one, prioritized based on time 
since capture, time away from moisture or heat sources, and apparent condition of the animal. 
Species of each animal was confirmed by literature and recorded, and weight, plastron and 
carapace length and width for turtles, snout to vent length for other species, sex, and age 
 
Muia 11
category were also recorded with the animal’s ID. Individuals large enough (such as turtles or 
larger snakes) were assessed for presence of a PIT tag, and, if not a recapture or previously PIT 
tagged, were then cleaned with antiseptic pads, injected with the tag, and the wound was covered 
with Liquid Skin agent to promote healing. After all data was recorded, animals were returned to 
exact capture site found by marked GPS points and released.  
This process of in-situ capture, in-situ data collection, transportation, ex-situ data 
collection, and release to wild was repeated once or twice daily for each day of each trip, besides 
the trip during the summer months, in which a different method of detection focusing on 
salamanders created an anomaly for this season in the entire study overall, as noted in the results.  
Data Analytical Methods 
 
Ex-situ analysis of all field-collected data was the second major aspect of this study. Data 
analytical methods following the completion of all of the trips analyzed multiple aspects of the 
results of the four-year herpetological survey.  
 
All data was input into Microsoft Excel separated by trip or year, as this is how the data 
sheets themselves were initially organized. Capture data was then separated by “season,” 
determined by month. Records from the end of March and beginning to mid-April were deemed 
as “spring,” the end of May and early to late June were deemed “summer,” and early October 
was deemed “fall.” This separation of year or trip and season designation would allow for the 
diversity and other measures as trends to be compared between the two different types of time 
period. Data input into Excel for each capture was pulled directly from the in-situ data sheets and 
included animal ID number, species designation, date of capture, time of capture, air temperature 
in degrees Celsius at the time of capture, and substrate temperature in degrees Celsius at the time 
of capture.  
 
Muia 12
After this initial data was input, total numbers, or abundance (N or n), of the two broadest 
types of herpetofauna (reptiles and amphibians) and each type of herpetofauna species 
(salamanders, frogs, turtles, lizards, etc.) were counted overall for all four trips combined and 
then separated by year or trip and then again by season, giving a total number of individuals 
captured for each year, for each season, and overall for the four year period. Pie charts were 
created from these totals, showing proportions of each species group relative to one another from 
the study overall, by year, and by season, and again showing proportions of each of the two 
broad types of herpetofauna relative to one another from the study overall, by year, and by 
season.  
Proportion (pi) of each species per year or trip was calculated by dividing the number of 
individuals in that group caught in each year by the total number of individuals overall caught in 
that year, as in the example below with skinks. 
Skinks as proportion (pi skinks) = number of individual skinks captured in the time period/total 
number of herpetofauna individuals captured in the same time period 
 This was done for each year or trip and then for each season. These proportions are all fractions 
of 1 so that the sum of all species detected in a particular time frame would sum to 1. The 
maximum proportion a species can exhibit during a particular time frame is 1, if that was the 
only species detected. Pie charts showing species proportion for each trip were created. 
Proportions of each broader type of herpetofauna (reptiles and amphibians) were calculated in 
the same manner, as below, for each year or trip and for each season.  
Reptiles as proportion (pi all reptiles) = number of total reptiles captured in the time period/total 
number of herpetofauna individuals captured in the same time period 
Pie charts were also created with these proportions as well as line graphs plotting proportion over 
time. Two lines were plotted, one for reptiles and one for amphibians, with year or season on the 
 
Muia 13
x-axis. These proportions had the same range of 0-1 with all species detected in a time frame 
summing to 1.  
Species richness was calculated for each trip or year and then for each season from the 
number of species that was detected during that time period. For instance, if in 2018 two snakes, 
one skink, and five turtles were caught, but no frogs or salamanders, the species richness for the 
2018 trip would equal 3. Species richness along with abundance were recorded for use in the 
next equations to find species diversity.  
Species diversity calculation was the next major assessment performed. Diversity indices 
are a mathematical measure of species diversity and the Shannon-Weiner Diversity Index 
equation was one utilized in this study. This index is one of multiple species diversity indices 
employed in the ecology field, yet it is particularly beneficial when estimating the diversity of 
species, or the heterogeneity, within an ecological community (Martensson 2016). The Shannon 
Index takes into account both species richness and relative species abundance, as mentioned, and 
better reflects overall community biodiversity than other ecological diversity indices (Briones Jr. 
2017). The Shannon Index value, or Shannon value, increases with diversity. The Shannon Index 
is also related to the concept of uncertainty. For example, if a community has very low species 
diversity, using the Shannon Index, the identity of an organism chosen by random can be 
determined with higher certainty or confirmed with a lower amount of uncertainty. If a 
community has a high diversity and an organism is chosen by random, there is greater 
uncertainty surrounding the identity of the species chosen, in other words, there is either low 
certainty or high uncertainty in this case (Wilson and Gownaris 2022). The Shannon Index was 
created on the basis of describing the “entropy,” or “disorder and uncertainty” of individual 
species in a community (Ekberzade 2022, Kaur 2020). The higher the uncertainty of the species 
 
Muia 14
identity of a chosen organism from the community, the higher the species diversity is implied in 
that community (Kaur 2020). Due to the nature of this equation, either a large number of species 
detected in the community, or a more even uniformity between the abundances of individual 
species detected in the community (species evenness) will increase the diversity index of that 
community. The equation for the Shannon-Weiner Index follows.  
 
 
For these reasons, the Shannon-Weiner Index was an appropriate calculation of species diversity 
in this study. Using species identification, overall species abundance (N), and species richness 
(S) for each time frame or community, the Shannon-Weiner value (H) is formulated by first 
calculating the proportion (pi) of each species, as calculated earlier in the study methods – 
dividing the number of individuals in the species detected in the time frame (year or season) by 
the total number of individuals detected in the time frame. For each species, that calculated 
proportion is then multiplied by the natural log of that proportion (lnpi). All of the values 
calculated for each of those species during the time frame are then summed and finally are 
multiplied by -1, giving the final Shannon Index value indicating degree of diversity using a 
degree of certainty (Wilson and Gownaris 2022). The Shannon-Weiner Diversity Index of values 
ranges from 0 to lnN, with 0 being the lowest possible and lnN, or natural log of the total number 
of species detected, being the highest possible species diversity in a given community 
considering that this value has a positive correlation with community biodiversity (Wilson and 
Gownaris 2022). If the individuals detected in a community were to all belong to a different 
species, the diversity index would reach its maximum, while if each individual detected were to 
belong to the same species, this index would be at its minimum value of 0 (Rain 2022, Wilson 
 
Muia 15
and Gownaris 2022). Any variations of amounts of individuals per species detected between 
those two extremes will return values between 0 and lnN, with most normal diversity values 
falling between 1.5 and 3.5 (University of Idaho 2009). In order to carry out these diversity 
calculations in the study, the already established columns of species groups, their abundance per 
trip year or season, the overall species abundance per trip or season, and the overall species 
richness per trip or season were utilized. In the manner described above, proportions were first 
calculated for each species group abundance in the 2018 trip and continuing through all trip 
years and then each of the three seasons. A Shannon-Weiner Index value was calculated for each 
of these time frames, acting as separate “communities” separated by time rather than physical 
location to rather assess diversity trends over a temporal rather than geological scale. After these 
values were calculated and recorded accounting for all species groups of herpetofauna detected, 
each time frame was then split into two separate charts of data, one with only the amphibian 
species and one with only the reptilian species. The Shannon-Weiner Index was then calculated 
in the same manner, resulting in a separate amphibian-only and reptile-only diversity value for 
each time frame of trip and season.  
 
In addition to the Shannon-Weiner Index of diversity, another frequently used diversity 
index in the ecological world was also performed on the data collected from this study. The 
Simpson’s Diversity Index exhibits several differences from the Shannon-Weiner Index, but is 
also valuable to include in ecological community surveys (Briones Jr. 2017, Wilson and 
Gownaris 2022). This index is based upon a measure of probability – the less diversity in a 
community, the greater the probability that two randomly selected individuals from that 
community will be of the same species (Wilson and Gownaris 2022). In the absence of diversity, 
 
Muia 16
if there were only one species present, the probability that the two individuals selected will be of 
the same species is 1. The equation of Simpson’s Index follows.  
 
 
Using species identification, overall species abundance (N), and species richness (S) for each 
time frame or community, the Simpson’s Diversity Index value (D) is formulated by first 
calculating the proportion of each species, as calculated earlier in the study methods and in the 
Shannon-Weiner Index – dividing the number of individuals in the species detected in the time 
frame (year or season, n) by the total number of individuals detected in the time frame (N). For 
each species, that calculated proportion is then squared. All of the values calculated for each of 
those species during the time frame are then summed. The value of Simpson’s diversity ranges 
from 0 to 1, but in a different way than the Shannon-Weiner Index. 0 in this case, due to the 
nature of the equation, represents infinite diversity and 1 represents no diversity, so the larger the 
initial value of D, the lower the diversity. For this reason, the Simpson’s Index value is often 
actually represented by 1-D, showing instead the diversity of the community on a scale from 0 to 
1, 1 representing maximum diversity (Wilson and Gownaris 2022). The initial D value was, for 
that reason, then subtracted from 1 to give the final Simpson’s Diversity Index value for each 
time period (trip or season) in the study. A Simpson’s Index value was also calculated for each of 
the time frames acting as separate temporal communities rather than community based on 
physical location to similarly assess diversity trends over a temporal rather than geological scale. 
The Simpson’s Index was also calculated in the same manner on the data split by broader 
amhibian and reptilian species, resulting in separate amphibian-only and reptile-only diversity 
values for each time frame of trip and season. Due to its nature, Simpson’s Index measures 
 
Muia 17
diversity using purely the relative abundance of each species in the community with each value 
showing the dominance or non-dominance of that particular species (Briones Jr. 2017). This 
index emphasizes more the common or dominant species in an index, while the Shannon-Weiner 
Index, as mentioned, better emphasizes and gives more weight to rarer species detected within a 
community (Smith and Berry 2010). Unlike the Shannon-Weiner Index, Simpson’s ignores 
species richness and equability as a factor into community biodiversity (Briones Jr. 2017). 
However, both indices are often employed together on such survey studies in order to assess 
community diversity using the different parameters and emphases of both measurements, and 
comparison between them is valuable to drawing conclusions on true community diversity as 
well (Beals et al. 1999, Briones Jr. 2017, Martensson 2016, Mohammed 2021). For this reason, 
both were calculated on the same data and their diversity values compared over the study 
timeframes.  
 
Species evenness was another parameter measured in this study in order to be analyzed as 
a trend over time. Species evenness refers to how close in number each species, or in the case of 
this study, each broader species group, in a community is. It refers to increased uniformity 
between the abundances of each species group detected to one another, and is another parameter 
used in ecological community studies to give a rough idea of diversity and to measure species 
dominance or rarity, the somewhat opposing force to diversity, in a community (Wilson and 
Gownaris 2022). Species evenness is calculated for a community or, in the case of this study, for 
each time frame of trip or season, by dividing the Shannon-Weiner diversity value for that period 
(H) by the natural log of S, the overall species richness for that period, as below (Wilson and 
Gownaris 2022). 
J = H/ln(S) 
 
Muia 18
This index was performed on all species groups for each time frame – trip and season. The range 
of values for species evenness is 0 to 1, with 1 indicating complete equability or uniformity 
between species detected in that community (Rain 2022).  
 
Finally, temperature as a parameter was assessed for this study, based on the strong 
relationship between herpetofauna species behavior and the temperatures of their environments. 
These averages would be used to compare to the measures described prior, such as abundance, 
diversity, richness, evenness, dominance and rarity, etc. that were calculated from this survey, 
and also in comparing findings with similar past studies from literature. Average temperature in 
degrees Celsius of each year or trip was calculated by adding each air temperature recorded at 
every capture during each trip or season, and then dividing that number by the amount of air 
temperature recordings taken. The same was done for each air temperature reading from each 
season, giving an average temperature for each season as well. Both the air and substrate 
temperatures, if recorded, for amphibians and reptiles were separated. In the same manner, an 
average air temperature, then an average substrate temperature, then an average overall 
temperature for amphibian species was calculated. An average air, then substrate, then overall 
temperature was calculated for reptilian species as well. The highest and lowest air and substrate 
temperature at a detection was noted for amphibians and then for reptiles for analysis uses. 
Substrate temperature was added at this point to assess another facet differentiating amphibians 
and reptiles: how they behave in response to temperature of the environment directly around 
them (the substrate they are conducting heat from).  
 
All of these calculations and recorded values were then placed into pie charts, line 
graphs, or tables where appropriate, and analyzed in context, comparing the expectations and 
 
Muia 19
predictions for the survey outcomes based upon cited literature and personal herpetological 
knowledge to what was actually observed over the four-year period.

Results 
In-situ Results 
 
Over the course of this four-year study period, a total of 86 herpetofauna individuals were 
captured, detecting 26 distinct species, or an overall species richness of 26. Reptilian species 
encompassed 18 of the 26 distinct species. Amphibian species accounted for the remaining 8

Discussion 
Again, the goal of this study was to detect and report the composition of herpetofauna 
species found in the study region of Northern Mississippi, and their diversity, abundance, 
dominance and rarity, richness, and evenness throughout the four separate survey trips in order to 
show trends in these measures over periods of time. The objective of this survey was to 
ultimately better inform the timing and methods for continuation and amplification of the survey 
in future years, to emphasize deviations from expectations for these parameters, give insight into 
the state of the herpetofauna community in the study region, create a baseline for comparison in 
continuation of the study, and note areas of conservational concern.  
Expectations 
Expectations for the outcomes of this survey were informed by broader herpetological 
distribution, ecology, life history characteristics, and presence in the particular study region. 
Firstly, while herpetofauna are distributed widely throughout the world, species prominence of 
both reptiles and amphibians is most notable in the warmer, more humid, temperate and tropical 
regions, particularly between 30 degrees N and 30 degrees S, although their ranges extend 
practically to every continent (Duellman and Zug 2022). The two groups only differ in that 
reptiles are usually more present in conditions such as extremely xeric deserts than amphibian 
species are (Duellman and Zug 2022). In the United States, this places the highest expected 
abundance and therefore variation of herpetological species in the desert, temperate, and 
subtropical ecosystems of the American south, southwest, and southeast (Olson and Saenz 2013, 
Valentine-Darby 2010). Mississippi in particular harbors a very diverse and abundant array of 
herpetofauna due to its location within that region of the country along with its diverse habitats 
throughout the state, affirming the site of this study as a prime location for such a herpetological 
survey into the future (Selman et al. 2018). Mississippi is known to have 30 endemic species of 
 
Muia 36
amphibians and 84 endemic species of reptiles, putting it among the very top states by amount of 
herpetofauna and consistent with the countrywide amphibian and reptile ratio, with prior 
surveying confirming the high herpetofauna presence in this state (Selman et al. 2018). 
The main drivers behind this global distribution of herpetofauna and expected abundance 
in the study region are some critical shared characteristics within the two groups of vertebrates. 
Herpetological species are ectothermic in nature, obtaining their heat from their environment 
rather than regulating body temperature internally. In addition, most species of herpetofauna are 
poikilothermic, using behavioral mechanisms to further regulate their temperature being obtained 
from their environment. All species of reptiles and amphibians have permeable skin as well. For 
these main ecological reasons, herpetofauna distribution overall is centered much more 
prominently around those warmer, wetter habitats and climates within the tropics, with 
distribution and variation lowering as you move away from those regions. These two groups 
require the aforementioned specific hygrothermal microclimates and environments within their 
habitats in order to develop, survive, and reproduce. These heat and moisture factors contribute 
to the expectation that more herpetofauna will be found in such regions as Northern Mississippi 
the most abundantly. These factors led to the expectation that the herpetological findings of this 
study would be robust, diverse, and will exhibit high presence of both amphibian and reptile 
species, with reptiles accounting for a larger proportion of detections, higher raw abundance, 
higher number of species, and also a wider diversity within those detections.  
Further expectations are be informed when addressing life history characteristics and 
ecology of amphibians and reptiles separately. Reptiles, unlike amphibians, have beta keratins 
within their epidermal cells, modifying them into scale structures on the outside of the skin, 
modifying their permeable skin to be significantly more resistant to desiccation than the much 
 
Muia 37
more permeable and vulnerable skin of amphibian species. Some reptile species, namely turtles, 
possess a shell as well, also resisting the water loss to the environment which amphibian species 
are more at risk of. Further, reptiles produce amniotic eggs while amphibians do not. This life 
history characteristic allows the embryo of reptilian species to be protected and nourished within 
their own “aquatic environment” of water and energy sources contained within a shell, while still 
remaining permeable enough to allow the exchange of gases with the environment. The eggs of 
amniotes such as reptiles allows for the independence from proximity to and reliance on water 
sources for reproduction, leading to the increased ability of reptilian species to inhabit drier and 
warmer habitats. Amphibians, on the other hand are non-amniotes. Eggs of these species lack a 
shell and amniotic membranes, rather possessing several gelatinous layers surrounding the 
embryo, requiring an aquatic environment for embryos rather than having a self-contained one. 
Amphibian species have gills at birth, further relying upon water for gas exchange in the embryo 
and larval stages (Cossel 1997). Most species develop lungs later in their life cycles while some 
retain their larval gills and remain fully aquatic. As a result, amphibian species require a water 
source and proximity to water for their reproduction, survival, and continuation. Due to this 
difference in ecological and life history characteristics, amphibians are characterized as being 
more highly temporal species, and measures of detection and diversity for them are expected to 
vary more dependent on time of year, season, weather, and even time of day, due to changes to 
temperature and moisture, as those are two critical facets of their life history and behaviors 
which are less limiting on reptilian species.  
This drastic difference between the two groups of herpetofauna is cause for different 
expectations concerning reptile and amphibian range, distribution, and detection in this study. 
The somewhat freeing of reptilian species from the dependence on water sources due to those 
 
Muia 38
mentioned characteristics assumes that reptilian species have a wider habitat and range for 
condition tolerance than amphibians. This assumption forms the expectation that the two groups 
will vary in detection through the study largely based on temperature and time of year as 
indicators to moisture level available to them. Reptiles are expected to be detected and show 
more dominance, diversity, and abundance overall at hotter temperatures and in specific seasons 
which have warmer temperatures or drier conditions, while this would be expected for 
amphibians overall at lower temperatures and seasons with wetter conditions. Due to that 
difference in ecological and life history characteristics, amphibians are characterized as being 
more highly temporal species, and measures of detection and diversity for them are expected to 
vary more dependent on time of year, season, weather, and even time of day, due to changes to 
temperature and moisture, as those are two critical facets of their life history and behaviors 
which are less limiting on reptilian species. 
While these overarching predictions exist based upon the major life history and 
ecological characteristics of these herpetofauna, expectations on detection and diversity arise 
also from other measures for this Northern Mississippi region in particular, such as species 
dominance and rarity. Predicted findings on overall herpetofauna and species abundance were 
informed by past studies and literature on Mississippi organisms. Snakes, lizards, skinks, and 
turtles are predicted to show the highest detection rates, abundance, and diversity in the study 
due to the dominance of these groups in the state of Mississippi overall and in the more northern 
regions specifically (Keiser 2018, Selman et al. 2018). There are almost triple the number of 
reptilian species in the state of Mississippi than the number of amphibian species, with the exact 
ratio of known reptilian to amphibian species being 2.8:1 (Keiser 2018). Within that group, 
snake species make up nearly half of all reptilian species, turtles make up about a third, and 
 
Muia 39
lizards make up about a tenth, accounting for the higher predicted detection and diversity of 
these more common groups in the study region (Keiser 2018). Meanwhile, a significantly lower 
proportion of amphibian detections and diversity is expected, as the rarest species in the state are 
both amphibious: salamanders and hellbenders (Keiser 2018, Mississippi Museum of Natural 
Science 2014).  
The meteorological averages of Northern Mississippi also informed predicted outcomes 
for the survey. May and June are the hottest months in the region with air temperatures 
maximizing around 31 degrees C and minimizing around 18.9 degrees C on average. October is 
close in temperature to mid-summer on average, with air temperatures maximizing around 24 
degrees C and minimizing around 10 degrees C. This is similar to the month of April, having 
maximum temperature around 23 degrees C and minimum around 9 degrees C. These months are 
all warmer than the averages for March, where air temperatures maximize around 18 degrees C 
and minimize around 4 degrees C (NOAA 2023). March on average expects the most days of 
precipitation, 9. This is followed by May expecting 8, April and June expecting 7, and October 
expecting 5 days of precipitation on average (NOAA 2023). Given these historical records of 
climate and weather averages for the region along with knowledge on herpetological ecology and 
life history, reptile detection and diversity were expected to be highest in the trips occurring in 
the months of the summer season, and lowest in the spring season based on average monthly 
temperatures (NOAA 2023). On the other hand, amphibian detection and diversity are expected 
to maximize during the fall and spring season based on average monthly temperatures as well as 
a precipitation average in the spring which is double that of the summer and late summer months 
(NOAA 2023).

Outcomes 
The outcomes of this herpetological survey were quite interesting and thought-provoking, 
providing information for timing and methods of future survey trips as well as calling for some 
explanation or assessment of potential bias in the study when compared to herpetological 
ecology, life history, and literature. 
The findings of this study met those general distribution-based expectations. The high 
raw abundance, increased amount of distinct species or species richness, similar species evenness 
throughout time periods, and presence of herpetofauna species in this state due to its latitude and 
overall climate was observed. High herpetofauna presence and expected detection rates were met 
and confirmed by the sheer amount of distinct species found in just the relatively short survey 
period. The major expected classes of amphibians and reptiles were all detected, with species of 
salamanders and skinks found to be dominant as was supported in literature on the region (Olson 
and Saenz 2013, Selman et al. 2018, Valentine-Darby 2010). As found through abundance and 
proportion calculations of both species and amphibians and reptiles overall, the expectation that 
reptiles would outnumber detected amphibians in abundance as well as amount of species was 
supported. The found ratio of detected reptiles to amphibians, 1.39:1, was lower than expected 
for the state of Mississippi overall, yet still exhibited the prominence of reptilian over amphibian 
detection for the state and for the country.  
Expectations on species presence, richness, dominance or rarity, and diversity overall and 
based upon season or climate were not all necessarily met. While herpetological species classes 
such as snakes, turtles, and lizards are the proven dominant species in the state and salamanders 
the rarest in the state, these classes did not end up exhibiting the expected dominance or rarity 
found throughout literature (Keiser 2018, Mississippi Museum of Natural Science 2014, Selman 
et al. 2018). Again, salamanders and skinks exhibited overall dominance, with the little brown 
 
Muia 41
skink, the southern cricket frog, and the southern two-lined salamander found to be the dominant 
species from each trip year, and the Mississippi slimy salamander, the southern cricket frog, and 
the little brown skink dominated detections during both seasons – all three during spring, and the 
little brown skinks in the fall. This outcome lined up well with the expectations formed on 
presence of reptiles and amphibians in each season, as the amphibian salamander species showed 
dominance in the spring where it was expected due to lowered overall average temperatures, 
while the reptile species, the skink, was the most dominant by a significant margin in the fall 
with the higher expected and observed temperatures on average.  
In comparing detection of reptiles and amphibians as classes, that overall ratio was as 
mentioned, a 1.39:1 favoring reptiles. However, the 2018 trip ended up showing the highest 
detection of amphibians, 2021 showed the highest detection of reptiles relative, and the other 
trips showed very close proportions relative. This observation did line up with expectations 
formed on seasonal climate averages as well as observed averages, as the amphibians were most 
commonly detected relative to the overall proportion in the cooler 2018 and 2022 season based 
on historical averages while reptiles were not most dominant in 2019 and 2021. These detections 
also lined up with the observed temperatures cooler in 2018 and 2022 and warmer in 2019 and 
2021. As for season, the expectation that reptiles will be more prominent in the warmer and drier 
fall and the amphibians in the cooler, wetter spring, based on climate histories, was met, and this 
also lined up with the climate data collected during the survey as fall did prove to be warmer 
than spring. Summer was indeed the warmest, but the detection data from this season was an 
anomaly so it was left out of conclusions on season presence. Herpetofauna species richness data 
findings overall only partially lined up with expectations in this way as well. The highest amount 
of distinct species was detected in 2018 followed by 2022 and then the other two trips equally,

showing the most species detected in the trips with the lowest overall observed average 
temperatures. The spring also showed slightly more (two) distinct species than the significantly 
warmer fall, displaying a larger contrast in overall herpetofauna species detection that had been 
predicted based on seasonal temperatures. The species evenness findings partially lined up with 
expectations, showing the least amount of evenness in 2018 (caused by the higher detection of 
amphibian individuals here) and the highest amount of evenness in 2022, as across the board 
detections did not favor one group over the other for that trip. However, the evenness of the 
spring was significantly higher than the fall, stemming from the much higher presence of 
reptilian species such as the little brown skink in the fall, which dominated detections over a 
number of other reptilian and amphibian species in that season. This finding implied that higher 
temperatures may cause a skewed detection of certain species over others, making for a less even 
community detected.  
Diversity was the next major measure, and expectations for this parameter were partially 
met by the findings concerning trip year and season. Overall, 2018 exhibited the highest amount 
of both Shannon-Weiner and Simpson’s diversity out of the trips, while 2021 exhibited the least. 
Spring showed the slightly higher Shannon-Weiner and Simpson’s diversity value than the fall 
did. This lines up with the higher abundance of species over all time periods, but only lines up 
with evenness findings in the seasons designation. The weighting of the abundances found in 
each particular trip outweighed the impact of evenness on these diversity calculations in that time 
period designation. This did not line up with the expectation that the community will be more 
diverse when the average climate is generally warmer due to herpetofaunal ectothermic nature. 
When the diversity, both Shannon-Weiner and Simpson’s, of amphibians and reptiles was 
assessed separately, it was found that, overall, reptile species had much higher diversity values

across years than amphibians. It was found that while amphibians dominated abundance in 2018, 
reptiles had a significant amount, and actually the highest value found overall, of diversity in that 
trip. This met the expectation due to herpetofaunal distribution and the known herpetofaunal 
makeup of the state of Mississippi that reptilian species would be not only more detected, but 
also show wider diversity of species among those detections. On the other hand, amphibian 
diversity did end up outweighing reptilian in the fall season by a slight amount. This was not

species detection in the community would narrow rather than expand during these warmer and 
some of the driest months of the year in this region due to the preferred cooler and wetter 
microclimates by this class.  
When assessing temperature data related to reptilian and amphibian detections separately,

that for reptiles, while substrate temperature at detection was lower. This substrate average lined

temperature average at detection did not. It was assumed that reptilian detection would yield a 
higher air and substrate temperature average, but this was not necessarily found to be true. 
However, when the summer anomaly of only salamanders detected was removed from the 
average temperature at detection findings for amphibians, this reduced the air temperature 
average at detection to almost the same as the reptilian average, making more sense and lining up

types of herpetofauna, it was found that reptiles were actually detected at slightly lower air 
temperatures than amphibians. However, when that anomaly season was again removed, the 
maximum air temperature at an amphibian detection was lowered to 25.9 degrees C rather than

29 degress C, again better lining up with expectations of cooler amphibian detections. The 
substrate temperature extremes at detection, however, lined up well with predictions, finding that 
reptiles were detected at a significantly higher maximum substrate temperature, and a higher 
minimum substrate temperature as well than amphibians.  
Informing Survey Methods 
The findings of this survey, again, are not only very intriguing when assessed compared 
to expectations on measures of these species and populations, but also are valuable information 
and a basis for planning on the timing and methods of future trips moving forward to also better 
contribute to this comprehensive survey goal.  
It was found that a trip regardless of time of year will return more reptilian detections and 
distinct reptilian species than amphibian. A spring trip will result in likely relatively more 
amphibian detections than one in the late summer or fall would. When temperatures are cooler 
on average, the amphibian detection rate and abundance will also increase, while reptilian 
abundance will also increase, but stay more consistent over the seasons. A wider diversity of 
amphibian species will more likely be detected in the fall than the spring season, however, and a 
wider diversity of reptiles will be detected in the spring than fall season, both despite predictions 
based on known climate (moisture level) and temperature preferences for the groups. A spring 
trip will also return a likely slightly higher amount of distinct species across the board than a fall 
trip will, yet the evenness between species detected will maximize by a large margin in the fall 
and will be much more skewed towards certain species in the spring season. Trips in months 
with lower levels of rainfall will likely result in more reptilian detections, while trips in months 
with the higher amounts of rainfall showed a more similar proportion of amphibian and reptilian 
detection and abundance to the observed proportions for the survey over the entire study period, 
or the average proportions being detected by the survey.

The optimal temperature range for maximizing the detection of herpetofaunal presence 
and species diversity would fall between 18 degrees C and 32 degrees C, indicated by the study

a fall trip will, while a fall trip will give a better insight into actual diversity of amphibian species 
in the region than a spring trip will, yet the spring trip will maximize detection of more distinct 
reptilian species. As for informing timing of this trip, a fall trip is definitely valuable to the 
detection of more distinct species across the board, particular the more dominant species in the 
region such as skinks, salamanders, and snakes. A later spring trip, however, would also 
contribute massively to the goals of the survey, allowing the incorporation of some amphibian

goals of the study and would establish a much more accurate and comprehensive survey of the 
region. Since summer data is still largely unknown due to the skewed results coming from a 
directed study once in this season, a trip with student assistance in the summer would also be 
valuable in filling in a gap in the data which currently exists and would most likely maximize the 
detection and species diversity of reptiles in particular found in the study region. Overall, the 
most comprehensive and accurate survey will combine efforts in each season, due to the 
observed variability in species and broader herpetological types across times of the year which 
have not been found to consistently line up with expectations informed on known ecology, 
distribution, and life history characteristics of the organisms.

Possible Biases 
Several potential biases have arisen as probable explanation for, or at least played a role 
in, the outcomes observed and for deviations from predicted detection and diversity based on 
known herpetological ecology and past literature findings. 
Firstly, Mississippi has been in a drought state in the past decade, beginning in 
approximately 2010 (Rasmussen 2022, USGS 2022). The Mississippi River was found to be at 
its record historical low in 2022 (Rasmussen 2022, USGS 2022). This is clearly a notable source 
of potential bias in the current and ongoing species survey in the study region. Abundances, 
detection rates, and species diversity measurements across the board are all likely significantly 
lowered and reduced, relative to a normal, healthy ecosystem in this region, due to these 
impactful drought conditions and the sensitivity of herpetofauna to alterations and disturbances 
to their environments (Dodd 1992, Martensson 2016, Ruthven et al. 2002, USGS 2022, Whitfield 
Gibbons et al. 2000, Winter et al. 2013). Further, the amphibian rates are likely more 
significantly impacted by this ongoing climate condition than reptilian species are, due to those 
drastic differences in vulnerability to reduced moisture levels and to habitat disturbance of 
environmental water sources. Furthermore, while the seasons lined up with temperature 
predictions relative to one another, overall all seasons ended up averaging at either the upper end 
of their normal average range per month, or were hotter than that past average. This is likely 
another symptom of the ongoing drought conditions in the study region and has likely also 
similarly affected the presence and diversity of herpetofauna but amphibian species more in 
particular, narrowing a likely more abundance and diverse community to a restricted and more 
threatened number. With both of these biases comes the difficulty to fully affirm this assumption, 
as the herpetological survey did not extend to before this drought and change to environmental 
 
Muia 47
temperatures began in the region, so it is difficult to compare findings with what should be 
observed in a healthier, balanced ecosystem.  
This outstanding source of potential bias in the study feeds directly into another larger 
source of bias in herpetological surveys worldwide in recent years: the issue of climate change. 
As herpetological species are, again, highly sensitive to altered temperatures and moisture levels, 
particularly in more temperate and subtropical regions instead of more fully tropical zones, the 
changes to Mississippi climate increasing with each passing year are definitely impacting the 
species and their abundances detected, as well as the overall composition of the Northern 
Mississippi study region (Olson and Saenz 2013, Rasmussen 2022, USGS 2022). Reproduction 
for herpetofauna are highly related to close time windows in specific seasons and condition 
ranges, with warmer spells for too long of a period of time having proven fatal across the board 
species-wise (Olson and Saenz 2013, Rasmussen 2022, USGS 2022). Altered thermal niches due 
to the changes to climate of the region are likely making the reproductive windows or range of 
suitable conditions of Mississippi and global herpetofauna successful breeding significantly 
narrower, skewing the results of such surveys on their populations and communities (Olson and 
Saenz 2013, Rasmussen 2022, USGS 2022). The increased agricultural intensification rates 
observed throughout the state of Mississippi are surely another source of habitat and conditions 
disturbance, posing a similar detriment to herpetological diversity in the study region and lower 
United States overall (Leyte-Manrique et al. 2019, USGS 2022).  
Further, methods of this survey in particular over the years thus far pose another source 
of bias to its findings. The visual encounters and by-hand disturbances and trappings are largely 
based upon human discretion in the trips thus far. Not all seasons of the year, summer in 
particular, are evenly represented in this survey, despite the known variations in detection and 
 
Muia 48
diversity that would be observed throughout a comprehensive, full-year study. An entire year 
was left out of this study due to the pandemic, 2020, and this gap in the data is likely a cause for 
making overall trends much more difficult to detect and to then compare successfully to future 
surveying in the region. The weather or precipitation amount was not taken into account or 
recorded for captures during this trip; its known that there was much more rainfall during 
specific trips than others, but this factor was not incorporated into the findings or discussion of 
the findings of this survey thus far, potentially skewing conclusions to be made on the impact of 
not only climate but more local weather conditions on the detection and diversity of 
herpetofaunal species in the study region. In addition, exact proximity to water bodies was not 
measured either or taken into account in any form in this survey thus far, possibly skewing 
detection toward reptilian and away from amphibian species due to an uneven amount of habitats 
or separate microclimates surveyed.  
Survey Improvements 
 
Clearly, numerous improvements can be made to this survey in trips going forward to 
better the detection and representation of all species actually present in the region. Additional in-
situ methods such as measuring and recording proximity to water for trap sites or hand-trapping 
sites, noting slope direction of detections in appropriate landscapes, and noting as well canopy 
cover, shade, or available sunlight factor would all lead to more comprehensive and accurate 
findings on the conditions for amphibians and reptiles as broader groups but also for differences 
in detection and diversity at the species level as well. Counting all individuals detected instead of 
just ones which had thorough examinations and measurements performed on them will further 
significantly improve the comprehensiveness of the study. Practicing consistency with laying or 
placing traps or detection sites throughout the study area by implementing a more thorough and 
organized pattern for trap sites, such as a grid fashion across the region, as well as increased 
 
Muia 49
amounts of trap sites overall, will greatly improve the success of detections along with reducing 
potential biases in trap site placements. In addition, classifying weather conditions and 
potentially substrate moisture level for each detection as opposed to only temperatures will 
further improve the survey and the quality of its findings and conclusions on herpetological 
presence.  
 
Additional ex-situ methods of data analysis, such as performing Chi-squared tests on 
specific species, will again return better conclusions on the presence of species relative to one 
another and to the entire study region. Adjusting diversity measurements for species importance 
is another method and measurement more recently incorporated into such species surveys (Ontoy 
and Padua 2014). By including a weighted value for importance of species to their community, 
informed, derived, and calculated by domains deemed important to conservation biology such as 
species endemicity, economic utility, functional role in the ecosystem, and IUCN risk status of 
the species (threatened or endangered), diversity indices such as Shannon-Weiner and Simpson’s 
are enhanced, with simulations in past studies confirming that a new index such as this 
successfully aids in conservation decisions particularly in cases where the Shannon’s indices of 
the ecosystems are equal or near equal, or in situations where the Shannon’s index clearly 
identifies a site but the relative importance of the species found in other sites is heavier (Ontoy 
and Padua 2014). This would be a very worthwhile inclusion and expansion for our ongoing 
survey in Northern Mississippi, assisting further in the accurate representation of not only the 
species but to areas of particular concern and to giving a more solid baseline for conservation 
awareness, attention, efforts, and prioritization going into the future.

Importance to Conservation  
 
This study has value moving into the future, especially concerning the changing status of 
herpetofauna globally. Surveys incorporating diversity indices and other measures of species 
composition in target regions provide important information about composition and structure of 
communities which holds particular value for the field of conservation biology. The ability to 
quantify diversity and species composition in this way has proven a critical tool for biologists in 
understanding community structure related to larger biodiversity conservation goals.  
Such studies as this survey, employing species diversity and related measures, have 
become major components to conservation planning more recently in the realm of ecology 
(Dodd 1992, Iknayan et al. 2014, Laurencio and Fitzgerald 2010, Moritz et al. 2005, Winter et al. 
2013). Monitoring of species diversity and the trends of other species measures are now 
fundamental for wildlife conservation, becoming abundantly more relevant to the field of 
conservation biology and have proven critical for evaluating the effectiveness of past 
management efforts as well as informing future management decisions (Baumgart, Martensson 
2016, Moritz et al. 2005, Winter et al. 2013). Species diversity indices estimate variation of 
species within and among systems, prioritizing species and habitat, informing actions and effort, 
and bridging research and actual conservation (Martensson 2016, Moritz et al. 2005, Winter et al. 
2013). Conservation planning in multiple instances globally and across the board species-wise 
has been accelerated and made more effective due to the incorporation of species diversity 
assessment and trends in related species measures (Martensson 2016, Moritz et al. 2005, Rabbe 
et al. 2022). Diversity indices – these mathematical models calculating number of species, 
distribution evenness, and species dominance with weighting in a particular community or 
compared across multiple have proven to inform management decisions in reducing overall 
biodiversity loss, overcoming difficult conservation targets, evaluating spatial diversity patterns, 
 
Muia 51
outlining detection, assessing levels and magnitude of disturbance, and prioritizing efforts to the 
appropriate species or habitats (Baumgardt et al. 2021, Gering et al. 2003, Ghosh and Basu 2020, 
Iknayan et al. 2014, Leyte-Manrique et al. 2019, Moritz et al. 2005). Herpetofauna have been 
one of the most prominent targets of such species diversity-informed conservation tactics 
globally as of late, with particular use and emphasis on species diversity indices to accurately 
assess composition, trends over time, conservation threat status, extent of habitat disturbance, 
and to inform species conservation efforts moving forward (Baumgardt et al. 2021, Dodd 1992, 
Ghosh and Basu 2020, Laurencio and Fitzgerald 2010, Leyte-Manrique et al. 2019, Moritz et al. 
2005, Rabbe et al. 2022, Russell et al. 2002, Ruthven et al. 2002). The value of this extended 
study thus far on a quite compromised group of organisms will prove critical in moving forward 
in their conservation, particularly with attention to bias and improvements to methods found in 
the four years incorporated moving into the future.
